labels.snapshot: For over 50 years, the MIT Outing Club's Camelot cabin has been a vital resource and center of the club's activities. Set on about 20 acres near Rumney, NH, Camelot hosts official club circuses, open cabins, and social events and is a base camp for individual club members using the cabin for personal adventures. Many MITOC members are first introduced to outdoor recreation and the club community through Camelot-based events.

labels.snapshot: The existing cabin is nearing the end of its usable life. Camelot was built in 1973, largely by MIT undergrads, and will not remain safe to sleep in for much longer. The new bunkhouse will give MITOC safe, comfortable sleeping space for 50 people.

Why a new bunkhouse
[shared text: SUM-2] [See more about the new bunkhouse.](/camelot/about)
Where things stand

Phase 1, which was finished in spring 2025, included construction of a new bridge, off-street parking lot, and access trail, as well as design and project support from architects, structural engineers, geotechnical engineers, mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) engineers, and MIT Facilities.

We are now raising funds for Phase 2, construction of the bunkhouse itself. We plan to break ground in late spring 2027 and finish in fall 2027, but construction can only start once the full $1.3 million is raised. [See how the money will be spent.](/camelot/about#funding)
Donate
We need your help to get there. If you are able, please consider donating to ensure MITOC can fulfill its mission for the next generation of MITOC members.
[Donate](/camelot/donate){: .bunkhouse-give-button .bunkhouse-give-button-small}
Questions? See the [FAQs](/camelot/faqs).

labels.snapshot: About
Camelot today

[shared text: SUM-1] The cabin is about 2.5 hours from Boston and currently sleeps about 30 people across the loft, living room, and kitchen. To visit, see the [Camelot rental page](/rentals/camelot).

Camelot’s loft had to be closed recently because it did not meet modern safety standards; it reopened only after a major repair effort by the cabin managers, and patches like this can only go so far. Making the existing cabin sleep 50 people would mean bringing it up to current code for lodging (sprinklers, fire-rated sleeping rooms, and emergency exits), and the cabin managers and the Town of Groton found no viable way to do that. Building new is the more cost-effective option.
The bunkhouse vision

After over a decade of planning, focus groups, discussions with MIT, and design work by Maclay Architects, we believe that building a new bunkhouse on the existing Camelot land is the best path forward. The new bunkhouse will be sited about 200 meters from the existing cabin and will provide heated sleeping space in a modern, safe, tightly insulated building enclosure.

**Who it’s for:** The bunkhouse supports MITOC’s goal of making outdoor recreation accessible, especially to new students, with inexpensive, year-round sleeping space that requires no experience or special equipment.
**Capacity:** The bunkhouse will sleep 50 people (five rooms of 10), enough for all but the busiest weekends of the year.
**Amenities:** The bunkhouse will have electricity, electric heat, and composting toilets.
**Fire safety:** A sprinkler system fed by a cistern in the basement, 1-hour fire-rated sleeping rooms, an emergency exit window in every room, and a networked fire alarm.

**No kitchen:** The bunkhouse will not have a kitchen. Building code requirements would have made including one prohibitively expensive. Instead, the existing cabin, expected to remain usable as a kitchen and lounge for another 10 to 20 years, will continue to be used for cooking.
For more information on the design of the bunkhouse, see [Project Details](/camelot/project).
The plan

From 2019 through 2021, the Outing Club worked with Maclay Architects to create a bunkhouse design that complies with all modern building codes, is satisfactory to MIT Facilities and the local town board, and yet maintains the wilderness ethos of the Outing Club and its Camelot property.
Timeline
**2011:** Discussions begin
**2013:** The MITOC Board of Directors (BOD) approves the project
**2014–2018:** Focus groups about club needs and the future of Camelot
**2018:** A generous initial donation in memory of Joris Naiman kick-starts active development
**2019–2021:** Design with Maclay Architects
**2022–2024:** Phase 1 fundraising (about $400,000)
**2023:** The Groton planning board approves the project
**2024–2025:** Phase 1 construction: a new bridge, off-street parking lot, and access trail, along with the final construction drawings
**2026–2027:** Phase 2 fundraising, now under way
**Planned for late spring 2027:** Groundbreaking! This requires raising the full $1.3 million
**Planned for fall 2027:** Construction complete!
Costs
The bunkhouse project will cost $1.3 million in total, based on 2026 quotes from general contractors for the finished construction drawings.

This includes construction of the new parking lot, which was necessary for Town of Groton approval; construction of the new access trail and bridge, which are necessary for construction vehicles and fire safety; construction of the bunkhouse itself; as well as design and project support work from architects, structural engineers, geotechnical engineers, mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) engineers, and MIT Facilities.

Phase 1 is complete. Donors gave about $400,000 for the new parking lot, bridge, and access trail, all finished in spring 2025, and for the final construction drawings. Thank you to everyone who made it possible!
Phase 2 is under way. The bunkhouse itself will cost about $900,000.
As of November 2026, $468,000 has been raised by 314 people toward the full $1.3 million. That leaves **$832,000 to go**, and we need the full amount before we can break ground in late spring 2027.
Gifts of every size count! [Donate online](https://giving.mit.edu/form/?fundId=3892696&amount=500), or read [more about costs and funding](/camelot/faqs#cost).
Bunkhouse team

Relaunched in Fall 2026, an eager committee of current MITOCers are spearheading fundraising and current project management! The fundraising committee includes graduate students, alumni, and affiliates who are MITOC trip leaders, board members, and lovers-of-Camelot.
David Lawrence ‘14 (former MITOC president and Camelot manager) and Greg Wallace (MITOC’s alumni liaison), who helped lead Phase 1, remain involved.

We have active participation from the MIT Department of Facilities, the MIT Division of Student Life, and the MITOC Board of Directors. To chat with us directly, reach out over email to [mitoc-bunkhouse@mit.edu](mailto:mitoc-bunkhouse@mit.edu).

labels.where: Project page: jump buttons under the title, one per section
labels.snapshot:
[Location](#location-on-the-property)
[Layout](#layout)
[Toilets and water](#toilets-and-water)
[Heating](#heating-and-insulation)
[Structure](#structure)
[Fire safety](#fire-safety)
Location on the property

The new bunkhouse will be located behind the existing cabin, about 200 meters up the hill. This is close enough that underground electrical wiring will be cost-effective, but far enough that sound from the cabin and campfire won’t carry. The bunkhouse will be farther from the property line than the existing cabin.
[img /images/bunkhouse/bunkhouse-site-plan.png] Bunkhouse site plan
Site plan, showing the parking area on North Groton Road, the footbridge over the brook, and the paths to the existing cabin, the lean-to, and the new bunkhouse.
Layout

The bunkhouse will have five sleeping rooms which accommodate 10 people each, so each room can hold a standard Winter School trip. A large central hallway contains ample space for gear storage for 50 people, including hooks, cubbies, and benches. The floor plan also includes a covered deck area. In MITOC tradition, we plan to decorate the walls in part with antique MITOC rental gear such as beavertail snowshoes and old skis!
[img /images/bunkhouse/bunkhouse-floor-plan.png] Bunkhouse floor plan
Floor plan: five sleeping rooms of 10 bunks each, a central hallway with gear storage and benches, three toilets, and the covered deck.
Toilets and water

Like the existing Camelot cabin, the bunkhouse will not have running water. Three composting toilets will be accessed from the covered porch (so that they are accessible to campers even when the bunkhouse is closed). The composter beneath the toilets will be located in a small insulated basement so that it remains warm enough to compost year round.
[img /images/bunkhouse/bunkhouse-section.png] Bunkhouse cross section
Cross section through a sleeping room (left), the central hallway, and the toilets (right), with the insulated basement below the toilets.
Heating and insulation

The bunkhouse will be tightly insulated and heating will not be required for most groups. Resistive electric heat will be provided to assist with initial heat-up on the coldest nights, but the energy-efficient structure means the bunkhouse won’t require much heat to stay warm once in use. Resistive heat makes sense for this application due to the infrequent demand and its high reliability and low cost.

MITOC’s current cabins (Camelot and Intervale) both require special training, in large part because of their heating (a wood stove and a finicky gas furnace, respectively). The bunkhouse’s electric heating alleviates these training and safety concerns.
Structure

To minimize site impacts, the bunkhouse will be an above-grade structure built on piers. A small basement and a section of poured concrete wall will provide the necessary shear strength. The remainder of the bunkhouse structure will be wooden.
[img /images/bunkhouse/bunkhouse-elevation.png] Bunkhouse elevation
Elevation, showing the covered deck, the piers, and the basement wall on the downhill side.
Fire safety

The bunkhouse will include a fire sprinkler system fed from a small cistern in the insulated basement. Sleeping rooms will be built as 1 hour rated fire enclosures, and each room will have its own direct egress window. The bunkhouse will have a networked fire alarm system. These measures ensure that the bunkhouse will comply with all modern fire safety codes.
Have more questions? See the [FAQs](/camelot/faqs).
Ready to help build the bunkhouse? [Donate](/camelot/donate).

labels.where: FAQ group heading (also the jump button). Page link: /camelot/faqs#why
labels.snapshot: Why a bunkhouse?

What is the long-term vision for the Camelot property?
The long-term vision is for Camelot to host groups of up to 50 people using two structures on the property: a sleeping cabin (the new bunkhouse), and a kitchen/lounge building (the existing cabin, or its future replacement). This gives us more flexibility to accommodate different groups on the property, and ensures that Camelot will remain available even while one of the two structures is closed for repair or replacement.

Why does MITOC need the bunkhouse?
Building a new structure at Camelot is the best way to ensure that the MITOC cabin experience will remain available to future generations of MIT students. The existing cabin is nearing the end of its usable life as a place to sleep. Its loft had to be closed recently because it did not meet modern safety standards, and it reopened only after a major repair effort by the cabin managers. Patches like this can only go so far. Today the cabin sleeps about 30 people across the loft, living room, and kitchen, and within a few years it will no longer be safe to sleep in. We will rely on the new bunkhouse to provide safe and comfortable sleeping space for 50 Outing Club members.

How does the bunkhouse support MITOC’s mission?
The core of MITOC’s mission is to make outdoor recreation accessible to all, with a special focus on new students who do not have previous outdoors experience. For this reason, it is important to have a place where MITOC members can sleep in all seasons which is inexpensive and does not require experience nor special equipment.

Why doesn’t the bunkhouse include a kitchen or lounge area?
We would prefer to have our sleeping space and living space in separate structures, which will improve the cabin experience for large groups with varied schedules. We believe that the existing cabin will continue to provide a serviceable kitchen and lounge for another 10-20 years, even once it's no longer used for sleeping, and having the bunkhouse in operation will ease the impact of its future replacement.

Can the existing cabin be brought up to code?
Not as sleeping space for a large group. Making the existing cabin sleep 50 people would mean bringing it up to current code for lodging, with sprinklers, fire-rated sleeping rooms, and emergency exits. The Camelot managers and the town of Groton found no viable way to do that, and building new is the more cost-effective option. With ongoing repairs and improvements, the existing cabin will remain suitable for use as a cooking and gathering space.

Why not buy a house instead?
The safety requirements for a structure that can legally sleep 50 people are quite different from the safety requirements for a single-family residence. The cost of the necessary modifications to a typical house would be a large fraction of the cost of building a new bunkhouse. We also want to preserve the special outdoor space and rustic atmosphere of MITOC cabins.

Why not buy new land for a bunkhouse somewhere else?
The current Camelot property meets the needs of the club. Although it is about an hour away from the higher peaks of the White Mountains, this distance does not pose difficulty for running hiking trips out of Camelot. We do not wish to give up on the existing improvements to Camelot nor our working relationship with the local authorities. And, we like the neighborhood, including the Rumney cliffs, Sculptured Rocks, and the wonderful new Green Woodlands preserve.

labels.where: FAQ group heading (also the jump button). Page link: /camelot/faqs#cost
labels.snapshot: Cost and funding

How much will the new bunkhouse cost?
The bunkhouse project will cost $1.3 million in total. That covers Phase 1 (the new parking lot, bridge, and access trail, and the final construction drawings, completed in 2025) and Phase 2 (construction of the bunkhouse itself). We updated this estimate in 2026, using initial quotes from general contractors based on the finished construction drawings.

What does the $1.3 million cover?
The $1.3 million covers the whole project:
* Construction of the new parking lot, which the town of Groton requested as a condition for granting our zoning exemption for the property.
* Construction of the access trail and bridge to the bunkhouse site.
* Initial site preparation.
* Construction of the bunkhouse itself.
* Design and project support from architects, structural and geotechnical engineers, MIT Facilities, and others.

The initial design work with Maclay Architects (Phase 0, 2019–2021) was funded and completed before the fundraising campaign launched, so it isn't part of the $1.3 million.

How will the bunkhouse be funded?
Construction of the bunkhouse will be fully funded by donations. Once completed, ongoing maintenance of the bunkhouse will be funded by user fees, in accordance with MITOC’s current practices. We anticipate charging about $10 per person per night, in line with the current cabin fee.

Camelot sees roughly 1,000 person-nights of use each year, about half of them from circuses alone. Spread over a 100-year lifespan, a $1 million bunkhouse works out to about $10 per person per night: the same as today’s cabin fee, and well below a bunk at a White Mountains hostel (from about $40) or a Randolph Mountain Club cabin ($30–$50). Unlike those, the bunkhouse will be reserved for the MITOC community.

labels.where: FAQ group heading (also the jump button). Page link: /camelot/faqs#timeline
labels.snapshot: Timeline and construction

What are the phases of the project?
* **Phase 0: design (2019--2021).** MITOC worked with Maclay Architects on the initial bunkhouse design. This was funded and completed before the fundraising campaign launched.
* **Phase 1: site work (2022--2025).** Fundraising from 2022 to 2024 raised about $400,000. In 2024 and 2025 we built the new parking lot, bridge, and access trail, and completed the final construction drawings for the bunkhouse.
* **Phase 2: the bunkhouse (2026--2027).** We're raising about $900,000 to build the bunkhouse itself, breaking ground in late spring 2027 and finishing in fall 2027.

When will construction start?
It already has! In spring of 2025, we completed Phase 1: the new parking lot, access trail, and bridge.

For Phase 2, construction of the bunkhouse itself, more fundraising is needed. We plan to break ground in late spring 2027, once the full $1.3 million has been raised.

How long will construction take?
The bunkhouse can be built in a single construction season, from about May to November. If we break ground in late spring 2027 as planned, the bunkhouse will be complete in fall 2027.

What construction method will be used for the bunkhouse?
The bunkhouse will be an above-grade wooden structure with exterior rigid insulation and back-ventilated cladding, supported by concrete piers and with a small concrete basement to house the fire sprinkler tank and toilet composters below the frost line.

Will students be involved in construction? Alums?
The new bunkhouse will be built by a professional general contractor, and their legal requirements for the worksite will require MITOC member participation to be structured and premeditated. Nevertheless, where possible, we plan to involve MITOC members in the construction process.

labels.where: FAQ group heading (also the jump button). Page link: /camelot/faqs#building
labels.snapshot: Building and site

Will the bunkhouse be heated?
The bunkhouse will be tightly insulated with modern building materials, and our calculations indicate that heating will not be required to maintain a comfortable temperature overnight. That said, the bunkhouse will be equipped with electric heat to assist with initial heat-up when the first occupants arrive on the coldest nights.

How long will the bunkhouse last?
We expect the bunkhouse to last about 100 years, allowing it to serve MITOC members for many generations to come. The design has been optimized for robustness in many different aspects: exterior rigid insulation (to maintain structural members at a controlled temperature and humidity), generous roof overhangs, and durable cladding materials, to name a few.

What about parking?
At the request of the town of Groton, we built a new gravel off-street parking lot with room for 20 cars as part of Phase 1, in 2024--25. While this added some construction cost, it improved our relationship with our neighbors and gives Camelot visitors a better place to park.

Will there be vehicle access to the bunkhouse?
Regular property users will continue to park their vehicles near North Groton Road and hike in about 200 meters to reach the Camelot buildings.  The bunkhouse access trail has steep grades and a loose surface, but seasonal access by construction vehicles may be possible.

labels.where: FAQ group heading (also the jump button). Page link: /camelot/faqs#people
labels.snapshot: Who's involved

Who's running the project?
The project is led by volunteers from the MITOC community, with active participation from MIT Facilities and the MIT Division of Student Life. The design is by Maclay Architects. For names and roles, see [Bunkhouse team](/camelot/about#leaders) on the About page.

Who should I contact with a different question?
Please email mitoc-bunkhouse@mit.edu.
Camelot Bunkhouse Fundraising

[shared text: SUM-1] The cabin was built in the 1970s on a shoestring budget, and it's nearing the end of its life as a place to sleep. We're now building a new bunkhouse on the property, with safe, modern sleeping space for 50 people, so that Camelot can keep serving MITOC for decades to come.

MITOC partnered with Maclay Architects to design a new bunkhouse for Camelot, which will be located about 200 meters from the existing cabin. The new bunkhouse will contain five bedrooms (sleeping 10 people each), a large central hallway, and a covered deck. The whole project will cost $1.3 million.

Phase 1 (a new parking lot, bridge, and access trail) was completed in 2025. We're now raising the rest of the $1.3 million so we can break ground in late spring 2027 and finish the bunkhouse in fall 2027. If you are able, please consider donating. This project will ensure we can fulfill our mission for the next generation of MITOCers.

labels.locator: paragraph starting "Camelot is a rustic cabin"
labels.snapshot: Camelot is a rustic cabin located near Rumney, NH. The cabin is situated on 20 acres of forest and can sleep groups of about 30 people. Camelot is a 2.5 hour drive from Boston and is within 15 minutes of Rattlesnake Mountain and the world-famous sport climbing at Rumney. The cabin is set back about 200 meters from the road and is only accessible by a rough foot trail.

The parking lot is a gravel off-street lot with room for about 20 cars. Vehicles must be entirely off the pavement. Park as close as possible to any other cars which are already in the parking lot. This maximizes capacity for busy weekends and also helps with plowing in case it snows during your visit.

labels.locator: paragraph starting "To pay for a cabin rental"
labels.snapshot: To pay for a cabin rental please head to the [Pay MITOC](/pay) page. **Cabin fees are non-refundable.** Do not pay for a visit until you have received permission to use the cabin from the cabin managers. The cost is $10.00 per person per night. (Camping costs $5.00 per person per night and is entered into the payment form as a 0.5-night stay.) Keyholders must pay for their entire group in advance and then collect payment from their guests. You may wish to consult the [Camelot Property Map](/docs/camelot/camelot_map.pdf) or the somewhat outdated [Camelot Manual](/docs/camelot/camelot_manual.pdf).
